# Generalized Linear Mixed Models

## Outline

- Hierarchical/ Multilevel Models
- Binomial GLMM
- Poisson GLMM


## Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM)

Recall: GLMs include fixed parameters, implying that each parameter was represented in each model as a single population value. 

::: callout-note
In GLMMs, some of the parameters are random, which means that they can take on different population values for different clusters of observations. Due to this mixture of fixed and random parameters, the model is known as a mixed model.
:::

::: callout-note
## Applications

GLMMs can be applied to crossover studies, longitudinal data analysis, observational studies, and non-Gaussian responses.
:::

## GLMM: Motivation

GLMMs provide a way to account for random parameters in the model. This way, we can account for variability at different levels of randomization. GLMMs can also allow the effects of certain predictors to vary across different levels, as well as inclusion of predictors that are specific to these levels.

::: callout-note
### Example
consider a data set consisting of a group of schools that were randomly selected from a population of schools (e.g., all schools in a district, state, or country), and a random sample of students that were selected from each school. Suppose that we wish to predict a binary variable representing a student outcome, such as whether a student will repeat a grade. 

- It is possible that students from the same school will be more similar to each other than to students from other schools in ways that may affect the outcome such as socioeconomic status, family’s education level and absenteeism.

:::

## GLMM vs. GLM vs. GEE

Using GLMMs present some advantages against traditional fixed effect models and GEEs.

::: panel-tabset
### vs. GLM

Traditional GLMs cannot account for the dependence of measured accounts within clusters. While they can model differences between clusters as a fixed parameter, it does not fully capture the variability between clusters in the calculated standard errors.

### vs. GEE

GEEs and GLMMs differ on how they account for correlated errors. GEEs use quasi-likelihood while GLMMs use Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) methods to estimate variance components.  In addition, it can only account fora linear overdispersion adjustments.

::: callout-note
GEEs also provide population-based averages because it is constrained to estimate the means of the marginal distributions due to how it accounts for correlated errors. GLMMs, on the other hand, are cluster-specific averages due to the use of conditional variances. GLMMs are ideal for use if we are interested on the effects for a typical member of the population.
:::

::: callout-important
Both GEEs and GLMMs are useful- it depends on the estimate you're interested in. 
:::

:::

## GLMM: Framework

There are two most common GLMMs: the random intercept model and the random slopes model. Suppose $X_{hij}$ corresponds to the value of a predictor $X_h$ for an individual $i$ in the $j^{th}$ group.

::: panel-tabset
### Random Intercept Model
For a link function $\eta_{ij}$ and $H$ total predictors, we introduce a random effect $U_{0j}$ that has zero mean and variance $\sigma^2_{u00}$.

$$
\eta_{ij} = \mu_0 + U_{0j}+ \beta_1X_{1ij} + \beta_2X_{2ij} + ...\\
\eta_{ij} = \mu_0 + U_{0j} + \sum_{h=1}^{H} \beta_hX_{hij}\\
U_{0j} \sim N(0,\sigma_{u00}^2) ~ i.i.d.
$$

This can also be expressed in distribution form. Suppose the outcome follows a Poisson distribution with rate parameter $\lambda_{ij}$,

$$
\eta_{ij} = \log \lambda_{ij} = \mu_0 + U_{0j} + \sum_{h=1}^{H} \beta_hX_{hij}\\
Y_{ij}|U_{0j} \sim Poisson(\lambda_{ij})\\
U_{0j} \sim N(0,\sigma_{u00}^2)~ i.i.d.
$$

### Random Slopes Model

We introduce random effects to each slope such that $\beta_{hij} = \beta^*_{hij} + U_{hj}$, where $\beta^*$ is a fixed slope and $U_{hj}$ is a random effect introduced to the slopes. The random effects follow a multivariate distribution:

$$
(U_{0j},U_{1j},...)^{T} = N(0,\mathbf{G})
$$

where $\mathbf{G}$ is the covariance matrix of the random effects.  
:::


## Estimating the Covariance Matrix

For GLMMs, there are two methods that can be used in estimating the covariance matrix: Adaptive Gaussian Quadrature and Laplace Approximation.

:::callout-note
In SAS, you can choose between the two methods. The quadrature method is more computationally expensive compared to the Laplace approximation but is more accurate.

In `R`, the default method used to estimate the covariance matrix is the quadrature method.
:::  
  
## Contrasts

You can still test any hypothesis with the form 

$$
H_0: C\beta = 0
$$

as a contrast with an approximate chi-square distribution under $H_0$. The degrees of freedom is equal to the number of rows of the contrast matrix.

## GEE: Notes


::: callout-note
## Missing data

Similar to GEEs, GLMMs can still provide estimates when the design is unbalanced due to missingness.
:::


## GLMM in `SAS`

- The `GLIMMIX` procedure can perform GLMM analysis. 
- The `RANDOM` statement adds random effects to the model.
  - Unless stated, the random effects are assumed to be uncorrelated.
  - The subjects can be identified using the `SUBJECT` option.
- GEE can be used for both binary and count data. When unspecified, it uses a Gaussian distribution.
  - `DIST` option can be used to specify distributions.
  - `DIST=BIN` uses binary
  - `DIST=POISSON` uses Poisson distribution to model count data



## GLMM in `R`

The `R` package `lme4` includes the `glmer` function. The random effects are included enclosed in parenthesis "(|)".

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(lme4)
mod1 <- glmer(outcome~predictor + (1|cluster),# random intercept
                data=sample_data)

mod2 <- glmer(outcome~predictor + (1+predictor|cluster),# random intercept and slopes
                data=sample_data)

mod2 <- glmer(outcome~predictor + (0+predictor|cluster),# random  slope only, fixed intercept
                data=sample_data)
```



## Example

The data shown is from a hypothetical study of the effects of air pollution children. Researchers followed 25 children and recorded whether they were exhibiting wheezing symptoms during the periods of evaluation at ages 8, 9, 10, and 11. The response is recorded as 1 for symptoms and 0 for no symptoms. Explanatory variables included age, city, and a passive smoking index with values 0, 1, and 2 that reflected the degree of smoking in the home. Use a random intercept model to account for the variability between children.

:::{.panel-tabset}

### SAS Data Set
```{.r}
data children;
   input id city$ @@;
   do i=1 to 4;
      input age smoke symptom @@;
      output;
   end;
   datalines;
 1 steelcity  8 0 1  9 0 1  10 0 1  11 0 0  
 2 steelcity  8 2 1  9 2 1  10 2 1  11 1 0
 3 steelcity  8 2 1  9 2 0  10 1 0  11 0 0
 4 greenhills 8 0 0  9 1 1  10 1 1  11 0 0
 5 steelcity  8 0 0  9 1 0  10 1 0  11 1 0
 6 greenhills 8 0 1  9 0 0  10 0 0  11 0 1
 7 steelcity  8 1 1  9 1 1  10 0 1  11 0 0
 8 greenhills 8 1 0  9 1 0  10 1 0  11 2 0
 9 greenhills 8 2 1  9 2 0  10 1 1  11 1 0
10 steelcity  8 0 0  9 0 0  10 0 0  11 1 0
11 steelcity  8 1 1  9 0 0  10 0 0  11 0 1
12 greenhills 8 0 0  9 0 0  10 0 0  11 0 0
13 steelcity  8 2 1  9 2 1  10 1 0  11 0 1
14 greenhills 8 0 1  9 0 1  10 0 0  11 0 0
15 steelcity  8 2 0  9 0 0  10 0 0  11 2 1
16 greenhills 8 1 0  9 1 0  10 0 0  11 1 0
17 greenhills 8 0 0  9 0 1  10 0 1  11 1 1  
18 steelcity  8 1 1  9 2 1  10 0 0  11 1 0
19 steelcity  8 2 1  9 1 0  10 0 1  11 0 0
20 greenhills 8 0 0  9 0 1  10 0 1  11 0 0
21 steelcity  8 1 0  9 1 0  10 1 0  11 2 1
22 greenhills 8 0 1  9 0 1  10 0 0  11 0 0
23 steelcity  8 1 1  9 1 0  10 0 1  11 0 0
24 greenhills 8 1 0  9 1 1  10 1 1  11 2 1
25 greenhills 8 0 1  9 0 0  10 0 0  11 0 0
; 
```

### R Data Set

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
children <- read.csv("children.csv")
glimpse(children)
children <- children |> 
  # across applies the same function to multiple columns.
  mutate(across(c(id,timepoint,age,smoke),~as.factor(.x)))
glimpse(children)
```


### SAS Code

```{.r}
proc glimmix data=children method=quad;
   class id city smoke age ;
   model symptom = city age smoke / solution
                   link=logit dist=bin ;
   random intercept / subject=id;
	lsmeans smoke/diff=all adjust=tukey ilink cl;
run;
```

### R Code

```{r}
library(lme4)
library(emmeans)
library(car)
mod1 <- glmer(symptom~city+smoke + age + (1|id), 
                data=children,
                family = binomial(link="logit"))

summary(mod1)
Anova(mod1)

emm_smoke <- emmeans(mod1,~smoke,type="response",infer=T)
emm_smoke
contrast(emm_smoke,method="revpairwise",infer=T)
```



### Answer

::: callout-warning
The results of `glmer` might not match the result of `GLIMMIX`.
:::

ID is the cluster/subject factor, hence we introduce a random ID effect. There is evidence of an association between wheezing and smoking ($\chi^2$=6.57, p=0.038). Applying the Tukey-Kramer adjustment, we observe strong evidence of a difference in wheezing between those with the highest smoking exposure (Smoking=2) compared to the lower values (Smoking=0). Those who recorded the highest smoking exposure where 7.35 (1.18-48.4) times as likely to exhibit wheezing compared to children with smoking index of 0.

There is no evidence of an association between wheezing and city ($\chi^2$ = 0.01. p=0.92), as well as age ($\chi^2$=3.68, p=0.30).

:::




## GLMM for Count Data

We can use the Poisson and negative binomial distributions to model count data.

::: panel-tabset
### SAS

We can call the Poisson distribution using `DIST=POISSON`. For negative binomial, we can use `DIST = NB`.

### R

In `R`, we can use `glmer()` for Poisson mixed models and `glmer.nb()` for negative binomial models from the `lme4` package.
:::

## Example

The data below shows the hospitalizations per person-year (`py`) change across 2019-2023 among patients who received the usual care and those who were assigned to care management. Use a Poisson GLMM with a random slope for years to test whether there are differences in the hospitalizations across the different groups.

:::{.panel-tabset}

### Data Set

```{r}
hosp <- read.csv("Hosp.csv")
glimpse(hosp)
hosp <- hosp |> 
  mutate(id=as.factor(id),
         yr = as.factor(yr))
```


### SAS Code

```{.r}
proc glimmix data=hosp; 
  lpy = log(py);
   class id group yr;
   model hosp_count = group  yr/ 
                     dist=poisson offset=lpy;
  random intercept yr/ subject=id; 
  lsmeans group/diff ilink cl;
run;
```

### R Code

```{r}
library(lme4)
library(emmeans)

mod_glmm <- glmer(hosp_count ~ group+yr+ offset(log(py)) + (1 + yr|id), 
       family=poisson(link="log"),
       data=hosp)

summary(mod_glmm)
Anova(mod_glmm)

emm_g <- emmeans(mod_glmm,~group,type="response", infer=T)
emm_g
contrast(emm_g,method="pairwise", infer=T)
```


### Answer
There is no evidence of a difference across the groups ($\chi^2$=0.55, p=0.46).

:::
